crm_note.headline: Mei Lin Tan completed second round at Fernhallow Capital (live Python and backtest case); awaiting feedback, consultant to chase Fri 2026-11-13
crm_note.how_it_went: Mei Lin did not give a view on the round as a whole. In the live Python hour she said having no access to the docs did not really hurt, as Nadia said she cared about the logic, and she raised survivorship bias from the disappearing names before computing anything. On the backtest case she thinks it landed well, but she said she was a bit hand-wavy on how she would model market impact for small caps.

rounds.format: Live Python with Nadia Osei (researcher, equities) on a provided laptop with no internet, preceded by a one-question probability warm-up. The session ran just over two hours in total, about two and a quarter, after starting late.
asked: Probability warm-up: a stick broken at two random points, what is the chance the three pieces make a triangle (Mei Lin answered a quarter)
Using daily prices and volumes for a few hundred stocks over about ten years, deliberately messy (series ending partway, gaps, bad prints), build a simple reversal signal and describe its performance
rounds.candidate_view: She said not remembering the exact groupby syntax did not really hurt: she said she would normally check the docs and wrote pseudo-pandas, and Nadia said that was fine as she cares about the logic. She thinks the real test was noticing the names disappearing, and she asked whether they were delisted or acquired, flagging survivorship bias. She had seen the probability question before and said so.

rounds.format: Case with Nadia Osei and another researcher, Pieter (surname not caught)
asked: Presented with a backtest with a Sharpe of about 2.1: what is wrong with this
How many variants had been tried to arrive at this one
How she would model market impact for small caps, and what participation rate
rounds.candidate_view: She covered look-ahead (trading at the same close used for the signal), costs and very high turnover, and multiple testing, including deflating the Sharpe for the number of trials. She thinks it landed well. They pushed on costs more than she expected, and she said she was a bit hand-wavy on market impact for small caps.

compensation.notes: She said she is not moving sideways. Compensation did not come up in the interview.

crm_note.notice_and_non_compete: Three months' notice and a six-month non-compete with paid garden leave. Nadia asked about notice and did not react.
competing_processes: Final round at a large multi-manager (pod) in the week starting 2026-11-16
risks: Final round at a large multi-manager in the week starting 2026-11-16 could produce a competing offer before Fernhallow decides
Three months' notice plus a six-month non-compete would push her start date well out
She is worried about depending on a small team built around the PM, Marcus, and what would happen to her if he left, having seen this happen to a friend

candidate.subject: Fernhallow Capital second round: next steps
candidate.body:
Hi Mei Lin,

Thank you for talking me through your second round at Fernhallow Capital in such detail.

Fernhallow usually take a few days to come back after the technical round, and I will chase them at the end of the week.

On your worry about the size of the team and what would happen if Marcus left: it is a fair question, and it would be worth asking Marcus directly at the final, as he is quite open about it.

I have noted your current package of a base of £135k with a last bonus of £50k, and your expectation of a base of about £155k plus bonus. I have also noted your final at the multi-manager next week and your early conversation at Draymoor.

Best wishes,
Hannah

client.subject: Mei Lin Tan: second round feedback
client.body:

process.format: Video call of about forty-five minutes. About ten minutes on your CV, then probability questions typed into a shared doc. No code.
process.who: Graham Lowe, senior researcher. He gives little feedback during the round, mostly moving on with "OK, next one".
process.what_they_look_for: Accurate probability reasoning, checking your own answers, and how you validate research: out-of-sample testing, how you handle crash periods, and who chose the holdout.

process.format: At the office, about two hours. First hour: one probability warm-up question, then live Python on a laptop they provide with no internet access. Second hour: a case where you critique a backtest.
process.who: Nadia Osei, a researcher on the equities side, for the first hour. Nadia and another researcher, Pieter (surname not caught), for the case.
process.what_they_look_for: Spotting problems in messy data before computing anything, especially series that stop part-way through. Clear logic over exact syntax. In the case: look-ahead, costs, turnover and multiple testing, with detailed questions on modelling costs.

process.format: Research presentation on a past project you can discuss without breaking confidentiality: thirty minutes to present, with presentation and questions taking about an hour together. Then thirty minutes on culture. A further fifteen-minute chat with the PM has also taken place, with the day running to about three hours in total.
process.who: Marcus Elling (PM) and two researchers, Nadia and Felix, for the presentation. Ingrid Saarinen, head of research, for the culture conversation.
process.what_they_look_for: Whether a signal survives neutralising against standard factors, why it works economically and who is on the other side of the trade, and a clear rule for when you would switch a signal off. Ingrid asked how you like to work and how you deal with being wrong.

examples: Expected number of rolls of a fair die until you see a six
Expected number of coin flips until you get two heads in a row
The same question for heads followed by tails
Three random points on a circle: probability the triangle contains the centre
A stick broken at two random points: probability the three pieces make a triangle

question_themes.theme: Deep dive on research from your CV
examples: How do you handle crash periods such as 2009 in your momentum work?
Did you test it out of sample properly, or tune it on the whole history?

question_themes.theme: Live Python on messy equity data
examples: Using daily prices and volumes for a few hundred stocks over about ten years, with gaps, bad prints and series that stop part-way through, build a simple reversal signal and say what the performance looks like
Shown a backtest with a Sharpe of about 2.1: "what's wrong with this"
How many variants do you think were tried to get this one?
How would you model market impact for small caps, and at what participation rate?
"Is this just value in disguise": have you neutralised against the standard factors?
"What would make you kill this signal": what evidence and what threshold would make you switch it off live?
How long would you wait? Would you sit through six months of drawdown?
Why does it work economically, and who is on the other side of the trade?
How do you like to work?
How do you deal with being wrong?

went_well: On the two-heads-in-a-row question, giving four, then correcting to six and walking through the states, drew "good, you checked it" from Graham Lowe.
In the Python task, asking why some series end (delisted, acquired) before computing anything, and noting that dropping them creates survivorship bias, drew a smile from Nadia Osei.

Not recalling the exact groupby syntax, saying "I'd normally check the docs here" and writing the intended logic in pseudo-pandas, drew Nadia's comment that this was fine because she cares about the logic.
On "is this just value in disguise", showing a backup slide with the factor-neutral version, where the effect drops but is still there, drew "OK, good" from Marcus Elling.
On when to kill a signal, saying it is better to cut the size than kill it outright, and to set the rule before going live rather than after, drew a lot of nodding from Felix.
tripped_people_up: Citing a holdout from 2019 onwards drew the follow-up of who had chosen it. It had been chosen by the researcher who built the strategy.
In the backtest case the interviewers pushed hard on costs: how to model market impact for small caps and what participation rate to assume. The answer given there was hand-wavy.
advice: For your second round, practise pandas work on messy price and volume data without internet access. If you forget the syntax, say so and write the logic clearly.
Before computing a signal on their data, check for series that end part-way through, gaps and bad prints, and say how you would handle delistings and acquisitions.
For the backtest case, work through look-ahead (trading at the same close used to form the signal), costs, turnover and multiple testing, including deflating the Sharpe for the number of trials.
Prepare a concrete approach to market impact for small caps, with participation rates you can defend. This is where the case pushed hardest.
Expect a probability warm-up at the start of the technical hour. Check your answer aloud, and if you have seen the puzzle before, say so.
Be ready to explain exactly how your past research was validated out of sample, including who chose the holdout and why.

For the final, bring backup slides showing your signal neutralised against standard factors. Have an economic explanation of who is on the other side of the trade, and a kill rule that is set before going live.
Do not read silence in the first round as a bad sign. Graham Lowe gives little feedback as he goes.
logistics: First round: video, about forty-five minutes, with a shared doc for working and no coding.
Second round: at the office, about two hours. Live Python is done on a laptop they provide, with no internet.
Final round: about three hours on the day, including a thirty-minute research presentation on any past project you can discuss without breaking confidentiality.
The firm asks about notice period and non-compete in every round: at the end of the first round, by Nadia Osei in the second round, and by Ingrid Saarinen in the final.
Ingrid Saarinen said it is company policy that the firm does not buy out garden leave. Your record shows 8 weeks' notice and a 3-month non-compete, so have the exact terms ready.
Marcus Elling asked for references at the final, before any offer.
Feedback after Graham Lowe's round usually comes within two days. After the technical it usually takes a few days.
